workingTitle: Chandra splits the most distant X-ray jet into two components
publicationStatus: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics on October 13, 2026; arXiv preprint submitted October 21, 2026.
coreFacts: The source PSO J030947.49+271757.31 is a blazar at redshift 6.10, seen when the universe was less than one billion years old.
The study combines 22 Chandra observations for 360.2 kiloseconds, about three times the previous exposure.
The extended jet region contains 84 detected X-ray photons against an expected local background of 12.7 photons.
The deeper image separates the extended emission into two slightly resolved components containing 40 and 29 photons, with expected backgrounds of 3.8 and 3.3 photons.
The extended emission is aligned with the known radio-jet axis and spans a region about 25 by 10 kiloparsecs in projection.
The jet's rest-frame 2 to 10 keV luminosity is about 1.3 times 10^45 ergs per second, roughly 18 percent of the core luminosity.
caveats: Chandra's photon count remains low, especially after dividing the jet into two components.
The data do not distinguish whether the X-rays arise mainly from synchrotron radiation or inverse-Compton scattering of cosmic microwave background photons.
The apparent spectral steepening between the two components has large uncertainties and cannot support a detailed claim about changes along the jet.
The unusually high jet-to-core luminosity ratio may reflect selection bias; the current high-redshift sample is too small for a redshift-evolution conclusion.
A simulation of a future AXIS-like mission is a forecast, not an observation.
